title: Why Do Jeans Have a Tiny Pocket Inside the Pocket?
parts: Did you find it? Inside the front pocket of your jeans, there is a tiny pocket.
Maybe you keep coins in it. Maybe a key. Maybe nothing at all.
It is too small for a phone and too awkward to reach. So why does it exist?
The answer has a pocket watch in it. And a patent. And a war.
Let's start with its name.
It is called a watch pocket. Yes, a pocket for a pocket watch.
A pocket watch is a watch you carry in your clothes, instead of on your wrist.
Levi Strauss and Company, the jeans maker, says the pocket was intended to store a pocket watch, which was typical in the late eighteen hundreds.
The word fob goes back even further. A dictionary of word origins says that in the mid sixteen hundreds, a fob was a small pocket in the waistband of breeches.
Fob pockets still turn up on trousers, waistcoats, and traditional jeans.
Now to the jeans. In eighteen seventy-three, Jacob Davis received a United States patent, shared with Levi Strauss's company.
Its title: Improvement in Fastening Pocket-Openings.
Davis was a tailor. Strauss had moved to San Francisco in eighteen fifty-three to open a dry goods business.
The trick was copper rivets. They kept the pockets from ripping, and made the openings stronger.
The company says the original pants had four pockets, and all of them were riveted.
Wikipedia, citing a news report, says the small watch pocket came a little later, in the late eighteen seventies. So the exact date is fuzzy.
Here is a funny thing. People call the watch pocket the fifth pocket.
But the company says that title belongs to the back left pocket, which did not appear on its jeans until nineteen oh one.
So when you say fifth pocket, the company's own article would disagree.
The rivets have a story too. In nineteen thirty-seven, the company began covering the back-pocket rivets, after customers complained that the copper points scratched furniture and saddles.
In nineteen sixty-six, the back rivets were dropped completely, because they kept wearing through even the toughest denim.
And during the Second World War, the company removed the rivets from the watch pocket, to save metal needed for the war effort.
So the smallest pocket has a wartime footnote.
Pockets themselves have a history. In the eighteenth century, the Victoria and Albert Museum says, women's pockets were separate garments, tied around the waist.
You reached them through openings in the gown. They carried letters, money, keys, handkerchiefs, even sewing kits.
For many women in the eighteenth century, a pocket was something you tied on, not something sewn in.
So why is the watch pocket still there? Honestly, the company's own article does not say.
Here is our reading. Once a design is everywhere, copying it is easier than changing it. That is an inference, not a documented reason.
Here is a safe guess. Today almost nobody carries a pocket watch, and people use the pocket for other small things.
So your jeans carry a little museum of old habits: a watch almost nobody carries, a patent for rivets, and a footnote from a war.
And if you keep a euro banknote in that pocket, take it out and turn it over. See the bridge? Is it a real bridge?
